newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian economy seen headed for abyss - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Albanian economy seen headed for abyss - analysts.

text.p: Economic transition sometimes happens at breathtaking speed. In the case of Albania, the transformation from star pupil of eastern Europe's emerging markets into the continent's pariah took less than a year.

Just days ahead of a general election, widely seen as the last chance to restore peace and order in this impoverished and chaotic Balkan nation, international experts said the task of rebuilding the economy from scratch appeared staggering.
"Whatever happens with the elections, we're in for a very rough ride for the rest of 1997," one top western diplomat told Reuters. "Things are bad now, but they're going to get worse."

After four months of bloody unrest sparked by the crash of five pyramid investment schemes earlier this year, Albania is a shattered nation. Its economy, barely three years ago the darling of the international investment community, lies in ruins, its institutional infrastructure in tatters.

Gross domestic product (GDP), which grew 10 percent in 1993, just three years after the country emerged from 45 years of hardline Stalinist isolation, is expected to shrink by at least the same amount this year.
Last year, GDP was estimated at a mere $2.3 billion. And according to government estimates, more than half of that was tied up in pyramid funds.
Inflation is raging and forecast to top 70 percent this year. The local currency, the lek, has shed 80 percent of its value against the dollar since the start of the year.

The mountainous country of 3.4 million people, the majority of which eke out a living barely above poverty level, has been thrown back to the point where it began its painful transition to a free market economy.

"Before 1990, this was the only country in Europe with a GDP per capita on an African level. Now, it's probably even worse," said Vladimir Gligorov, Albania expert at the Vienna Institute for Comparative Studies.
"Nothing is really changing in a positive direction. The evidence suggests that the situation is getting worse and worse," he added.
Industrial production is almost at a halt, with most of the heavy industries once supplied by China or the Soviet Union shut down.

The few functioning plants are hit by supply shortages, frequent power cuts or damaged by the wave of violence and looting that swept the nation following the collapse of pyramid schemes in which many people lost their life savings.
The schemes, which depended on continuing to attract fresh investment to fund big payouts, collapsed when confidence in them stability evaporated.
The armed unrest that has swept most of the country has even prevented some desperately needed humanitarian aid reaching remote villages and hamlets.

A 7,000-strong international protection force, dispatched to guard aid convoys, has made little difference. Much aid still ends up in the hands of gangs controlling parts of the country or is syphoned off by local officials, observers say.
In a country with little democratic tradition, political parties have been quick to blame each other for the bleak economic reality.

The Socialists, the reformed communists standing against President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party in Sunday's election, say his free-market government did too little too late to rein in the shady pyramid funds whose collapse sparked anarchy.

Berisha, waging an aggressive campaign to help his Democrats defend the overwhelming majority they won in last year's poll that was widely seen as flawed, has accused the Socialists of fomenting the violence an attempt to retain power.
The Socialists currently lead a multi-party interim government formed in March.
Whichever side emerges as the winner from the two-round poll faces an uphill struggle to assert its power.
"The real problem is the redistribution of power. It will be an extremely difficult task for any central government to take over the country," Gligorov said.
"The elections don't really mean anything, even if participation is decent and they are free and fair," he added. "I'm extremely pessimistic about the future."
